newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - EU says Alitalia cash is state aid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU says Alitalia cash is state aid.

text.p: The European Commission has ruled that a huge recapitalisation of troubled Italian flag carrier Alitalia must be classed as state aid and not a market investment, a Commission spokeswoman said on Friday.

Under European Union law, a government can only give cash to firms under strict conditions, but Italy's loss-making flag carrier has already accepted numerous EU penalties in return for the desperately-needed money and hopes to avoid further demands.

Italy requested Commission permission last year for a capital injection worth some 3.3 trillion lire ($2 billion) to rescue the debt-laden airline and the government has handed over 1.5 trillion lire of the funds.

The centre-left coalition has argued that the cash does not amount to state subsidies because it is acting in accordance with its rights as a shareholder and has been promised a fixed return on its money like any normal market investment.
"It will be considered as a state aid," spokeswomen Sarah Lambert told a news conference in Brussels, adding that the EU executive would decide on any aid-approval conditions before the end of July.

Alitalia bowed to EU pressure earlier this year to cut back its network as part of the recapitalisation plan, reducing its fleet of planes by 14 and cutting some 27,000 flights a year, or 10 percent of operations, off its timetables.

It also promised that it would not offer the lowest price on any route to avoid charges of state-sponsored dumping and indicated that it would accept just 2.8 trillion lire of funds from the government instead of the expected 3.3 trillion.
"We are fundamentally convinced that there cannot be any more conditions placed on this plan," said one official at Alitalia, who declined to be named. "We have already accepted so much."
The Italian government, which controls the airline through state holding company IRI, declined to comment on the EU decision until the full findings were released next month.

"We are working to provide Alitalia with a future. The company will close its accounts well this year and needs capital. We are committed to giving it (money)," Transport Minister Claudio Burlando told reporters. "I will say no more."

Alitalia's managing director Domenico Cempella vowed in April to press ahead with the recapitalisation, despite reported criticism of the project by the European Commission, saying it was bringing the firm back to health.

The airline, which chalked up its ninth straight year of losses in 1996, agreed to a rescue package with unions last June after months of bitter battle over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

Commercial director Federico Nucci said earlier this month that Alitalia's current performance was ahead of forecasts. "If we can continue in this actual trend we will not close 1997 at breakeven, but with a significant profit," he said.
However private sector competitors, including British Airways, have complained about provisions for government money to be pumped into the struggling group.

Alitalia argue that the Commission has recently given the green light for state help for Air France, Spain's Iberia and Greece's Olympic Airlines, and say that it would be unfair to impose tough new conditions for the Italian flag carrier. $1 = 1,698 lire
